title: Points for Plastic: Wecyclers Takes Cargo Bikes into Lagos Streets
dek: In 2012 a Lagos-born MIT graduate started collecting recyclables by bicycle and paying households in points, because few people knew what recycling was.

story.event: Launching household recycling collection by cargo bicycle in Lagos, with households rewarded in points
story.summary: In 2012 Bilikiss Adebiyi-Abiola, a former IBM software engineer who developed the idea in an MIT class, co-founded Wecyclers in Lagos to collect recyclables from low-income households using locally made cargo bicycles. Households earned SMS points per kilogramme, redeemable for food, goods, phone credit or cash, and the company sold sorted materials to factories with support from the Lagos Waste Management Authority. By 2014 it served about 5,000 households; in 2015 it was still small and not yet profitable.
paragraphs: In a development ventures class at MIT's Sloan School of Management, Bilikiss Adebiyi was set a project: find something that would tangibly help people at the bottom of the economic pyramid. She had grown up in Lagos and spent five years as a software engineer at IBM, and she chose waste, which she had seen everywhere at home. Lagos produced about 10,000 tonnes of rubbish a day, and only about 40 per cent of it was collected. Her project team also saw that manufacturers needed cheaper raw materials. In the class, she later said, she met others who wanted to do something about waste. In 2012, back in Lagos, she and her co-founders launched Wecyclers.

Two choices shaped it. Instead of trucks, collectors rode locally made cargo bicycles, called wecycles, which were cheap and could get down crowded, rutted streets. And instead of appealing to civic duty, Wecyclers paid households: every kilogramme of plastic, cans and water sachets earned points, sent by text message, that could be exchanged for food, kitchen goods, phone credit or cash. "Recycling is not common," she told the news agency AFP. "People don't even know what recycling is." Of the points, she said: "The incentive was a way to get the conversation started."

The city's waste authority, LAWMA, authorised the collections and lent the company ground in Surulere where the sacks were sorted before being sold to factories. By February 2014, about eighteen months in, Wecyclers had collected nearly 200 tonnes from about 5,000 households and employed about 30 people. A tailor in Surulere told AFP that before, her area had been "very dirty, smelling everywhere".

It stayed slow, small work. In 2015 Voice of America found Wecyclers in two neighbourhoods, handling 40 to 50 tonnes a month, less than one per cent of the city's daily waste, and not yet profitable. That year the Case Foundation backed it with $55,000, and in 2019 it won the King Baudouin Foundation's African Development Prize, worth 200,000 euros.

quote.text: Any object not interesting in itself may become interesting through becoming associated with an object in which an interest already exists. The two associated objects grow, as it were, together: the interesting portion sheds its quality over the whole
quote.work: Talks to Teachers on Psychology; and to Students on Some of Life's Ideals
quote.source_title: Talks To Teachers On Psychology; And To Students On Some Of Life's Ideals, Project Gutenberg eBook #16287
quote.connection: Wecyclers did not ask Lagos to love recycling first. It tied the sacks to rice, phone credit and cash. James, writing for teachers, explains why that can work: interest borrowed from something wanted spreads over the dull thing until it is cared about too.

reflection: Adebiyi did not wait for her city to care about recycling. She attached it to things people already wanted and trusted that cleaner streets would make their own case later. James would say that is not a trick; borrowed interest can become real interest.

Think of something you need others to do that does not interest them for its own sake: recording a result properly, writing down a near miss, turning up to a short meeting. Lecturing rarely changes it. Linking it honestly to something they already value, an easier week or a thank-you that names exactly what they did, often does.
invitation: Choose one dull task you want a colleague to keep doing, and find one thing they already care about that you could honestly link it to. Try that link once this week and notice what happens.

cross_checks.claim: Wecyclers was launched in Lagos in 2012, from an idea developed in an MIT Sloan class.
Collection used cargo bicycles, and households earned points per kilogramme redeemable for goods, phone credit or cash.
LAWMA authorised and supported the work, including space for sorting.
Lagos produced about 10,000 tonnes of waste a day, with about 40 per cent collected.
Wecyclers won the King Baudouin Foundation's African Development Prize (2018-19).

research_notes: Household and job counts vary with date and source: about 5,000 households and about 30 staff (AFP, February 2014); 'more than 5,000 households' and 52 staff (Lionesses of Africa, January 2015); 7,000 households and 75 jobs (MIT Better World, undated); over 10,000 households and over 100 jobs (D+C interview, undated). The story uses only the dated AFP figures and VOA's 2015 description, and the edition makes no claim about final scale. Collection vehicles: most sources say cargo bicycles; True Africa and Al Jazeera say tricycles; the story says cargo bicycles, as Adebiyi did to D+C. Co-founders: sources say she started Wecyclers 'with her cofounders' and MIT Better World names a classmate surnamed Fallon; no full name was found, so co-founders are not named. Funding is treated as mixed: sponsors and LAWMA support at launch (AFP), grants and prizes (Cartier Women's Initiative 2013, Case Foundation 2015, King Baudouin 2018-19) and sales of recyclables; no equity round is documented. The King Baudouin prize is dated 2018-19 by The Benchmark and reported as recent in April 2019 by Al Jazeera; the story says 2019. The Benchmark says she stepped down as chief executive in 2017 for posts in the Lagos State government; this is left out because no second source was checked. The Guardian Nigeria profile, Engineering for Change, BET and the Tony Elumelu Foundation pages do not load for the verifier. William James's passage is from his lecture to teachers on children's interests and is applied here by analogy.
